entity_title: TTOL work permit — apply from abroad
fact_text: A third-country national coming to Finland to work for a Finnish employer needs a residence permit for an employed person (TTOL); a confirmed job is required first and the FIRST permit must be applied for from abroad — only extension applications can be filed inside Finland.
evidence_quote: If you apply for this permit as a first residence permit, you must submit the application abroad.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can enter Finland and then sort out the work permit. Actually the first TTOL must be filed from outside Finland with a confirmed job already in hand; only extensions can be filed in Finland. Action: apply from the home country before travelling.

entity_title: TTOL is tied to a field of employment
fact_text: A residence permit for an employed person (TTOL) is granted only for the specific field of employment to which the job belongs, and the holder may work only within that field (they may hold several jobs in the same field).
evidence_quote: A residence permit for an employed person is granted for the field of employment to which your job belongs.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a work permit lets you take any job. Actually a TTOL is locked to one occupational field. Action: if the employee may switch sectors, check whether a new permit is needed before changing jobs.

entity_title: Labour market test for work permits
fact_text: A residence permit for an employed person may be subject to a labour market test: the employer must establish whether suitable labour is available within a reasonable time in Finland or the EU/EEA before a third-country national is hired for the role.
evidence_quote: the employer must establish if there is available labour force within a reasonable time in Finland or within the EU/EEA for the work in question

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed hiring a foreign worker is purely the employer's choice. Actually a TTOL can require proof that no Finnish/EU/EEA worker was available (availability consideration). Action: the employer should document the recruitment/availability assessment before applying.

entity_title: Employer certification unlocks the D visa
fact_text: If the employer holds employer certification, a work-permit applicant can apply for a D visa at the same time as the residence permit. The D visa (up to 100 days) lets the employee travel to Finland immediately after a positive permit decision, without waiting for the physical residence permit card to be mailed abroad.
evidence_quote: If your employer has obtained employer certification, you can apply for a D visa at the same time as you apply for a residence permit.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you must wait for the residence permit card to be posted abroad before travelling. Actually with a certified employer plus a D visa you can fly to Finland right after the decision. Action: check whether the employer is certified and apply for the D visa alongside the permit.

fact_text: To qualify for a specialist residence permit (or an EU Blue Card), the third-country professional's salary must be at least EUR 3,937 per month in 2026, in addition to holding the required higher qualifications or special expertise.
evidence_quote: your salary is at least EUR 3,937 per month in 2026

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed any skilled job qualifies for the faster specialist track. Actually there is a specific minimum monthly salary (EUR 3,937 in 2026) that is updated yearly. Action: confirm the offered gross monthly salary meets the current-year threshold before choosing the specialist or Blue Card route.

fact_text: Specialist and EU Blue Card applications can use Finland's fast-track service, which aims to issue the permit in about two weeks — far quicker than the standard employed-person (TTOL) permit.
evidence_quote: You can apply for this residence permit via the fast-track service and get the permit in two weeks.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed all Finnish work permits take months. Actually specialists and Blue Card holders can get a roughly two-week fast-track decision. Action: route senior/skilled hires through the specialist or Blue Card permit to compress timelines.

fact_text: A person employed as a specialist may work in Finland without any residence permit if the work lasts a maximum of 90 days (entry/visa conditions may still apply).
evidence_quote: Specialists may work without a residence permit if the work lasts for a maximum of 90 days.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed every day worked in Finland needs a residence permit. Actually a specialist can work up to 90 days permit-free. Action: for short assignments under 90 days, check the specialist exemption instead of filing a full residence permit.

entity_title: EU Blue Card is not tied to one employer
fact_text: An EU Blue Card issued by Finland is not bound to a certain employer and requires the highly qualified job to last at least six months — unlike the field-locked residence permit for an employed person.
evidence_quote: Your permit is not bound to a certain employer.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a Finnish work permit ties you to the sponsoring employer. Actually the EU Blue Card is portable across employers (subject to conditions), while a TTOL is locked to an occupational field. Action: for mobile senior talent, prefer the Blue Card for employer flexibility.

fact_text: The first residence permit for an employed person (TTOL) costs 750 EUR filed electronically versus 950 EUR on paper (extension 230 EUR electronic / 430 EUR paper); the paper channel is the more expensive one.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed paper and online applications cost the same. Actually the paper TTOL costs 950 EUR against 750 EUR online. Action: file in the Enter Finland online service to pay the lower fee and speed processing.

entity_title: Foreign key employee flat tax at source
fact_text: A qualifying foreign 'key employee' can have wage income from a Finnish employer taxed at a flat tax-at-source rate instead of progressive tax, even while resident in Finland for over 6 months. The rate fell from 32% (until 2025) to 25% from 2026; because the source tax is final, no deductions are available.
evidence_quote: Until 2025, the tax withheld at source from key employees was 32%, and starting in 2026, it is 25%.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed foreign professionals always pay Finland's progressive income tax. Actually eligible key employees pay a flat 25% (2026) source tax on salary. Action: apply for a key-employee tax card to lock the flat rate instead of progressive taxation.

fact_text: The foreign key-employee flat tax requires a cash salary of at least EUR 5,800 a month (fringe benefits excluded), work requiring special expertise, and that the person has NOT been a resident taxpayer in Finland in the 5 preceding calendar years; the tax card must be requested within 90 days of starting work and the relief lasts a maximum of 84 months.
evidence_quote: Your cash salary for your duties as a key employee is at least €5,800 a month.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the flat key-employee tax is open to any well-paid expat. Actually you need at least EUR 5,800/month cash salary, special expertise, no Finnish tax residence in the prior 5 years, and must apply within 90 days. Action: verify all conditions and file the key-employee tax card within 90 days of the start date (relief caps at 84 months).

entity_title: Kela coverage is not automatic on arrival
fact_text: Moving to Finland does not automatically give a third-country worker Kela (social insurance) coverage: if a residence permit is required, it must be granted before the person can qualify for Kela benefits, and coverage then depends on being considered a permanent resident or on working in Finland.
evidence_quote: if you need a residence permit granted by the Finnish Immigration Service (migri.fi) to stay or work in Finland, you must get one before you can qualify for benefits from Kela.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed arriving in Finland automatically enrols you in Kela social security and a Kela card. Actually you must first hold the required residence permit and be either working or a permanent resident. Action: after the permit is granted, notify Kela of the move and apply for a Kela card; short/temporary postings may get limited or no coverage.

entity_title: Non-EEA driving licence is only temporarily valid
fact_text: A non-EU/EEA driving licence is only temporarily valid after moving to Finland: a licence from a Geneva/Vienna Convention (Contracting) state must be exchanged within two years of moving, while a licence from another Finland-recognised state is valid only one year after moving; after that it no longer entitles you to drive.
evidence_quote: When two years have passed from your moving into Finland, you are no longer entitled to drive with your foreign driving licence.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a foreign driving licence stays valid as long as it is unexpired. Actually after moving to Finland you have only 2 years (Convention state) or 1 year (other recognised state) to exchange it, and exchanging a non-EU/EEA licence needs a medical certificate. Action: start the Traficom licence exchange well before the deadline.

fact_text: To bring family members to Finland on the basis of family ties, the worker (sponsor) must usually meet a secured NET income requirement that scales with household size and region — e.g. in the Helsinki metropolitan area EUR 1,210/month for one adult plus EUR 610 for a child; income based on social assistance or unemployment benefits does not count.
evidence_quote: For a family consisting of 1 adult and 1 child who live in Helsinki (group 1), the income threshold is EUR 1,210 + EUR 610 = EUR 1,820 per month.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a work permit automatically lets your family join you. Actually family-tie permits require proof of sufficient net income scaled by family size and city (higher in Helsinki), and benefits do not count. Action: confirm the sponsor's net salary meets the regional threshold for the whole household before applying.
